papers.title: Variable penetrance of schizophrenia in 22q11.2 deletion syndrome is associated with impaired, but reversible, neuronal mitophagy.
papers.summary: This paper investigates why only some people with 22q11.2 deletion syndrome develop schizophrenia, linking the risk to defects in mitophagy, the process by which neurons clear out damaged mitochondria. The researchers found that neurons from affected individuals show impaired mitophagy, and importantly, this defect could be reversed experimentally. This suggests a potential therapeutic target for preventing or treating schizophrenia in genetically at-risk populations.
papers.why: This work directly connects impaired neuronal mitophagy to psychiatric disease risk, offering a mechanistic model highly relevant to studying mitophagy dysfunction in neurons and interneurons within the broader context of brain disorders.
papers.figure: Figure showing comparative mitophagy flux/markers in patient-derived neurons from penetrant vs non-penetrant 22q11.2DS carriers, before and after rescue treatment.

papers.title: Inferring single-cell gene expression profiles from multicellular spatial transcriptomics data with st2sc
papers.summary: This paper presents st2sc, a computational method designed to infer single-cell level gene expression profiles from spatial transcriptomics data where each spot contains signals from multiple cells. It likely uses deconvolution or deep learning-based approaches to disentangle mixed cellular signals into individual cell-type contributions. The goal is to achieve single-cell resolution insights from data that would otherwise only offer averaged, multicellular readouts.
papers.why: This tool could help resolve cell-type-specific gene expression within mixed neuronal populations, which is critical for distinguishing interneuron subtypes and their molecular states in spatial transcriptomics datasets relevant to mitophagy and perineuronal net research.

papers.title: CosMxScope: scalable reconstruction and digital pathology integration of imaging-based CosMx spatial transcriptomics data.
papers.summary: CosMxScope is a computational tool designed to reconstruct and scale imaging-based CosMx spatial transcriptomics data for easier analysis. It integrates this spatial transcriptomic data with digital pathology images, allowing researchers to link gene expression patterns to tissue morphology. The tool aims to make large, imaging-based spatial datasets more manageable and interoperable with standard histological workflows.
papers.why: This tool could help integrate spatial transcriptomics data with tissue imaging in brain sections, supporting analysis of interneurons and perineuronal nets in their spatial context alongside mitophagy/autophagy-related gene expression.

papers.title: Spectrast: a multiscale spatial statistics toolkit for single-cell spatial transcriptomics
papers.summary: Spectrast is a newly described computational toolkit designed to analyze spatial transcriptomics data at multiple spatial scales within single cells and tissue contexts. It provides statistical methods to quantify how gene expression patterns relate to spatial organization across different distance ranges. This allows researchers to detect spatial patterns, such as gradients or clustering of transcripts, that might be missed by single-scale analyses.
papers.why: This toolkit could help analyze spatial transcriptomics data around interneurons and perineuronal nets, revealing multiscale gene expression patterns relevant to mitophagy and autophagy processes in specific brain microenvironments.

papers.title: Urolithin A plus EGCG enhances mitophagy associated pathways, mitochondrial dynamics, and bioenergetic function in humanized amyloid-β knock-in mice.
papers.summary: This study tested a combination of Urolithin A and EGCG, two natural compounds, in mice genetically engineered to produce human-like amyloid-beta plaques, a hallmark of Alzheimer's disease. The treatment improved mitophagy (the clearance of damaged mitochondria), mitochondrial dynamics, and overall energy production in brain cells. These findings suggest the compound combination could help restore mitochondrial health in a neurodegeneration model relevant to Alzheimer's disease.
papers.why: This paper directly addresses mitophagy and mitochondrial bioenergetics in a neurodegenerative disease model, offering mechanistic insight and potential therapeutic targets relevant to the mitophagy focus of the PhD project, even though it does not use spatial transcriptomics or interneuron/PNN-specific analyses.
papers.figure: A figure showing quantification of mitophagy markers (e.g., PINK1/Parkin, LC3-II, mitochondrial dynamics proteins) and bioenergetic measurements (e.g., oxygen consumption rate) across treatment groups would be most informative.

papers.title: Early Treadmill Exercise Promotes Neurological Recovery and Parkin-related Mitochondrial Quality Control After Ischemic Stroke.
papers.summary: This study examines whether early treadmill exercise after ischemic stroke can improve neurological recovery in an animal model. It focuses on Parkin, a key protein that tags damaged mitochondria for mitophagy, and whether exercise enhances this mitochondrial quality control process. The findings suggest that exercise-induced activation of Parkin-mediated mitophagy may help clear damaged mitochondria and support neuronal recovery after stroke.
papers.why: This paper reinforces mechanistic understanding of Parkin-mediated mitophagy in neurons under injury conditions, which is directly relevant background for studying mitophagy regulation in brain neurons more broadly.
papers.figure: Figure showing Parkin and mitophagy marker expression (e.g., LC3, PINK1/Parkin colocalization) in peri-infarct neurons across exercise vs. sedentary groups.

papers.title: Microbial peptidoglycan activates mitophagy via binding autophagy adaptor p62 to reduce liver fibrosis.
papers.summary: This paper shows that a microbial cell wall component called peptidoglycan can trigger mitophagy, a process that clears damaged mitochondria. It does this by binding to p62, a protein that acts as an adaptor connecting damaged cell components to the autophagy machinery. In a liver fibrosis model, this peptidoglycan-induced mitophagy helped reduce scarring, suggesting a gut-liver-microbiome axis influences liver disease through mitochondrial quality control.
papers.why: While focused on liver tissue, this paper provides mechanistic insight into p62-mediated mitophagy signaling that could inform how similar autophagy adaptor pathways are studied in neurons.
